abstract: Objective. Altered intracranial pressure (ICP) is a key biomarker for traumatic brain injury (TBI). However, obtaining ICP measurements is a highly invasive process. Heart rate variability (HRV) has demonstrated potential as a useful biomarker for ICP changes, but few studies have investigated the relationship between ICP changes and HRV. This work examines how HRV and ICP interact in cases of TBI and whether HRV metrics can be informative of the state of autoregulatory control at elevated ICP. Approach. Electrocardiogram signals were recorded in seven non-human primates under anesthesia. ICP changes were induced by means of fluid increase via a cannula in the ventricles. Time- and frequency-domain HRV metrics were calculated from ECG and correlated with physiological indicators including CPP, ICP, and pressure reactivity index (PRx). Main results. Results demonstrate that there is no direct linear relationship between HRV and ICP. PRx and HRV, however, revealed a significant group level relationship where the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) increased after a clinically significant PRx threshold, implying that HRV may be more closely associated with TBIs in terms of autoregulatory changes rather than ICP changes. Significance. This study provides insights into changes in brain physiology in response to ICP increases by demonstrating the relationship between CAR and HRV. Further, this work draws attention to conflicting reports in the literature when interpreting the interaction between HRV and other physiological variables.
